analysis.one_liner: Bans unregulated soft money from federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House committee it was sent to; a broader soft-money ban did become law later in the same Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Federal Election Campaign Act to bar anyone from spending money to influence a federal election unless that money follows the limits, prohibitions, and reporting rules that apply to regular campaign contributions. In plain terms, it outlaws soft money — unlimited checks from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals funneled through national party committees, outside the normal contribution caps and disclosure rules. It applies to elections after January 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain because campaign money would have to flow through channels with contribution limits and public disclosure, rather than unlimited soft-money checks that neither cap nor fully disclose who gave. Candidates and parties competing without access to huge soft-money checks also gain a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits spending any funds to influence a federal election unless those funds are subject to the contribution limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements of the Federal Election Campaign Act, which is how it bans soft money.

Soft money was the channel that let corporations, unions, and wealthy donors give unlimited amounts through national party committees, outside the caps and disclosure that apply to ordinary contributions; the bill closes that channel for federal elections.
The ban takes effect for elections occurring after January 2001.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees would lose the unlimited soft-money stream they used for issue ads, party building, and voter contact. Large corporations, unions, and the wealthiest donors would lose their biggest unrestricted channel for influencing federal elections. Broadcasters and political consultants who sold or produced soft-money advertising would lose that business.

drawbacks.text: Soft money also paid for party-building work such as voter registration and grassroots organizing; a ban removes that funding even if some of it benefited ordinary participants rather than big donors.

A federal soft-money ban alone can push money toward outside groups and issue advertising that the bill's FECA-tied reporting rules may not fully capture, so the money could reappear in less accountable channels.

The bill contains a single enforcement provision with no additional disclosure machinery for state-level party activity, so compliance would rest on the existing Federal Election Commission structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: closing the unlimited, weakly disclosed soft-money channel is the most direct campaign-finance reform available to Congress, and it costs ordinary people essentially nothing. The honest objection is design risk — money pressured out of party committees historically migrated to outside issue groups, and this short bill relies entirely on existing FECA machinery to hold the line. On balance the upside for voters outweighs those risks, though a stronger bill would have addressed the outside-group escape route.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended — though a broader soft-money ban became law in 2002 through a different bill (the McCain-Feingold campaign finance law).

narrative.text: Patsy Mink of Hawaii introduced the bill on January 30, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who funded soft money were better off while the bill sat unused — though their position eroded when a broader soft-money ban became law in the same Congress.

for.name: Rep. Patsy Mink
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban soft money in federal elections and gave introductory remarks.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled action; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Too few members acted to reveal a partisan split: only two Democrats cosponsored and no votes were ever taken, though soft-money fights in this era split both parties internally.

industries.note: Parties raised unlimited soft-money checks for federal campaigns through this channel; the bill cuts it off and subjects party spending to contribution limits and public reporting.

industries.industry: Large corporations, unions, and wealthy donors
industries.note: Soft money was their largest unrestricted route for influencing federal elections; the bill eliminates it for federal races.
Soft money financed large issue-ad buys on television and paid production and consulting work; banning it removes that revenue stream.
